items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: he introduced me to Ellington, James P. Johnson, Art Tatum, Louis Armstrong

ctx.x: I couldn’t miss it. I couldn’t go to bed. I lived on 130th and Seventh Avenue. Art Tatum was playing on 131st Street, Don Redmond was playing across the street at 132nd Street, Billie Holiday was singing at 138th Street at a place called the Yeah Man Club, there was Small’s Paradise on 135th Street. Everything was in Harlem. You know you could walk, and I walked so much ‘till I just passed out. I just couldn’t miss anything. So everybody was, you could see everybody that you wanted to see in the daytime on…

Club. It was just, it was amazing and it held my, I was just in awe at all of these people that I had seen on the stage in Columbus, Ohio at a dance. Cab Calloway. Here I am walking down Seventh Avenue, and looking at these people and saying hello to them. And Count Basie introduced me to all these people. He was like a father. When I first joined the band I was 19 and he just took a liking to me and he introduced me to Ellington, James P. Johnson, Art Tatum, Louis Armstrong, oh my goodness. It was just…
At the time you joined the Basie band, how much of the music was written out?

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: But they were all beautiful friends of mine, but to be playing with Duke Ellington, gee whiz.

ctx.x: Well, you did record with Duke on that wonderful back to back…

That was one of my greatest moments. Norman Granz called me and wanted me to make this album. I said, oh man, did I want to do it, what a thrill. There was Johnny Hodges, I’d never played with him, never played with Duke. Jo Jones was on the record date and Joe Benjamin had played with my band when I first went to New York in the Birdland so I had played with him. But they were all beautiful friends of mine, but to be playing with Duke Ellington, gee whiz.
Do you remember that particular date, how it was to work with him in the studio?
No, I meant about the reading and everything? You could --

Yeah. Yeah, yeah, but it still wasn't -- you know, it took a lot of rehearsals to get what you wanted to get. And they had one guy, Chappie Willett, he used to write such hard arrangements it would take so long to get these players together. And musicians could read in those days, because Don Redman had a fantastic band. So did Duke. So did Jimmy Lunceford. So did Fletcher, Fletcher had a good band and he always wrote in the hard keys. That's why all the good musicians came out of Fletcher's band, you know.

In fact, all the musicians in those days were good musicians. They knew how to read. [But Basie's band was based on head arrangements because everybody took solos in Basie's band. Basie's band wasn't an ensemble band. It was noted for soloists, you know. Everybody was a fantastic soloist.]
